conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m glad we have a chance to talk today. 

To get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions about the past seven days, and it helps us see if you might be experiencing the common “blues” of new motherhood or something that could use a little extra support.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand how you’re really doing so we can be sure you have the help you need. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy things or look forward to events the way you normally would—like a favorite show, a phone call with a friend, a quiet cup of coffee—or has that enjoyment slipped?

Honestly? Most of the things that used to feel fun just feel kind of… flat. I’ll put on the show I used to love, and five minutes in I’m scrolling mindlessly or thinking about everything that could go wrong with the baby. Same with coffee—I used to savor the quiet, but now I’m gulping it down just to keep my eyes open and my mind still races. I do still look forward to my best friend’s nightly check-in text; when the phone buzzes I feel a tiny spark. But even that joy feels muted, like someone turned the volume way down.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I still laugh sometimes—like, my partner made a dumb joke about diaper explosions the other night and I actually giggled—but it feels kind of forced, like the laugh runs out of gas halfway through. Most of the day I’m just too tired or tense to find the humor in anything.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. When I think about tomorrow—or next week—it’s mostly a heavy feeling, like “how will I even get through it?” I used to get excited over little plans, like a walk to the coffee shop or my mom coming to visit, but now they just feel like chores I have to survive instead of something nice ahead.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby spits up a ton after feeding, my brain jumps straight to “I must’ve eaten something wrong” or “I’m not burping him right.” When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. I caught myself thinking, “A good mom would know how to fix this.” I know, rationally, babies just cry—but in the moment it feels like proof I’m failing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there with the baby sound asleep and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet—so I’m tiptoeing to the bassinet every five minutes to check his chest is moving. Or I’ll imagine the stroller tipping, or the dog barking waking him, and I can’t shake the picture once it starts. There’s no real reason, it just barges in and parks itself in my head until something else distracts me.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week, yeah. Once I was just folding laundry and suddenly felt like I couldn’t get air—my chest went tight, heart pounding, had to sit on the floor and grip the couch leg until it passed. No warning, no real trigger, just this wave of “something awful is about to happen.” It’s scary enough that I avoid being upstairs alone now, in case it hits again while I’m holding the baby.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Yesterday the baby needed feeding, the trash was overflowing, my phone was ringing, and I just stood in the kitchen staring, paralyzed, tears welling up because I didn’t know which thing to grab first. I keep telling myself, “Take one task,” but even that feels impossible, like every chore brings three more behind it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening almost every night this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain starts replaying every little thing I might have messed up—did I fasten the swaddle tight enough, did I skip burping that one feed—and I can’t shut it off. It takes me over an hour to drift off, then I’m up again around two or three, heart pounding, checking the monitor. By morning I feel like I’ve barely slept at all, even when the baby actually gave me a four-hour stretch.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… most of the day, most days. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel this heavy ache in my chest for no reason, or I’ll catch myself just staring out the window with tears coming. It isn’t constant—sometimes I’ll get distracted for a few minutes—but the sadness keeps sliding back in like a gray fog I can’t outrun.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Mm-hmm… maybe twice this week. Yesterday it was because the baby wouldn’t nap and I felt like I’d tried everything—rocking, the swing, white noise—and when I finally set him down he started wailing again. I just sat on the floor with him in my lap and cried, too. It feels like the tears come out of nowhere, then I’m embarrassed that I can’t keep it together.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…Yeah. Once or twice, just a quick flash—like, “What if I just kept walking past the turn to our house and didn’t come back?” or I’d picture the kitchen scissors and feel this jolt of fear that I could do something stupid. I never want to act on it, and I’d never leave my baby, but the idea pops in and scares me. I shove it away as fast as it comes, but it’s been happening.

Hearing how your days have been since the baby arrived, I sense the heavy fog you're living under: joy feels distant, ordinary tasks loom like mountains, and worry or sadness slip in without warning. You're working so hard to be a devoted mom, yet you're also carrying relentless self-blame, nightly dread, and scary thoughts you'd never choose. Please know many new mothers feel overwhelmed, and reaching out is a strong, courageous step.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughs occasionally but describes the laughter as forced and short-lived, indicating a marked reduction in ability to find humor.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing upcoming events as heavy burdens rather than sources of enjoyment.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, pervasive self-blame for normal infant behaviors, indicating guilt occurs "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, disproportionate worries without real cause, matching "very often"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes two sudden, intense panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (chest tightness, pounding heart) and avoidance behavior, aligning with "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, paralysis, and inability to cope with routine tasks, matching "Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty sleeping due to racing thoughts and anxiety, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness throughout most of each day, with frequent tearfulness and a persistent 'gray fog' feeling that returns quickly after brief distractions, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive passive self-harm thoughts occurring "once or twice" with vivid imagery, matching "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The patient scored 25 on the EPDS (cut-off ≥14 indicates probable major depression). She endorses core symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med>: daily low mood, marked loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), excessive guilt, frequent crying, sleep disruption, impaired concentration, and feelings of being overwhelmed. She also describes panic-like episodes meeting possible <med>panic attacks</med>. Item 10 indicates occasional passive suicidal thoughts without intent. This pattern, duration, and functional impairment warrant urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist
2. Request depression-specific therapy such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</med> with a perinatal-trained therapist
3. Begin safety-planning: identify 24/7 supports and crisis hotline (e.g., 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline)
4. Mobilize practical help-ask partner, family, or friends to handle night feeds or household tasks so you can rest
5. Practice brief soothing activities you enjoy (walk, music, shower) when agitation rises; keep them short and doable
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after starting supports
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety (self-report EPDS-style items)

Symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation (“everything feels like a chore”)  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt (“I’m failing”)  
- Daily free-floating anxiety, intrusive catastrophic images  
- Two discrete panic episodes this week (sudden dyspnea, chest tightness, fear of collapse)  
- Overwhelm/paralysis with routine tasks; feels “drowning”  
- Sleep initiation problems linked to rumination; fragmented overnight sleep despite infant stretches  
- Spontaneous crying spells, often situation-triggered  
- Fleeting passive self-harm ideation (“keep walking,” visual flash of scissors) – NO intent/plan

Pattern: Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥2 weeks; interfere with functioning and infant care.

Screening significance: High likelihood of major depressive episode with anxious features; possible panic attacks; safety risk flagged by self-harm cognitions.

Risk factors: First-time motherhood, sleep deprivation, absence of perceived support, prior anxiety traits (noted).

Recommendation: Complete EPDS immediately; same-day safety assessment; consider expedited referral to perinatal psychiatry/psychotherapy and mobilize support resources.
